cards.title: Public-coin canonical isomorphism with a GI-oracle prover
cards.formal: Does graph-isomorphism search have a constant-round public-coin pseudodeterministic interactive proof whose honest prover runs in deterministic polynomial time with an oracle for the graph-isomorphism decision problem? More precisely, ask for a fixed integer r, a polynomial-time public-coin verifier V without an oracle, one uniform deterministic polynomial-time GI-oracle prover P, and a function s selecting one isomorphism for each ordered isomorphic pair of labeled graphs, such that: with P, V outputs s(G,H) with probability at least 2/3 on every isomorphic pair; with every possibly unbounded malicious prover P′, V outputs either s(G,H) or ⊥ with probability at least 2/3 on every isomorphic pair; and on every nonisomorphic pair it outputs ⊥ with probability at least 2/3 against every P′. The number of exchanged messages is at most r on every execution. The probability is over the verifier’s public coins and, when applicable, the malicious prover’s coins.
cards.why: Tests whether removing verifier secrecy necessarily raises the computational work required of an honest prover, even for a basic graph search problem whose solutions are efficiently checkable. It separates mere existence of an interactive proof from the resources needed to participate in one.
cards.status_note: Read the original definitions, graph-isomorphism theorem and conclusion; checked the full arXiv version and the February 2022 thesis’s explicit question on page 44. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no matching protocol. The 2026 work on pseudodeterministic quantum query algorithms addresses a different model and is not a resolution of this classical interactive-prover question. Searches are not exhaustive.

cards.definitions:
An instance is an ordered pair (G,H) of finite simple undirected graphs on the labeled vertex set [n]={1,…,n}, n≥1, given by binary adjacency matrices. Their total encoding length is N=Θ(n²), including n. Graphs of different orders can be rejected immediately. An isomorphism is a permutation π:[n]→[n] such that {u,v} is an edge of G if and only if {π(u),π(v)} is an edge of H. The output encodes π by the list (π(1),…,π(n)); ⊥ is a separate rejection or failure symbol. The function s is fixed for the protocol, depends only on the ordered labeled input pair, and always selects a valid isomorphism. It need not be lexicographically first, and it is not required to be invariant under relabeling. The quantifier is ∃s,V,P,r working for all pairs, not a choice of s after observing the prover or random transcript.

The GI decision oracle takes an explicitly encoded pair of finite simple graphs and returns 1 exactly when they are isomorphic. The honest prover P is one deterministic oracle Turing machine, with a polynomial bound in N on total computation and written query length over an interaction, for every legal verifier transcript. Each oracle answer is charged one step; writing its query is charged ordinarily. The prover may make polynomially many adaptive queries on graphs of polynomial encoding length, but receives no advice, isomorphism witness oracle or stronger decision oracle. This is the usual P^GI honest-prover bound. Only the honest prover is computationally limited: canonical soundness and nonisomorphism soundness must hold against all strategies, including unbounded provers.

The verifier is a uniform probabilistic bit algorithm with total running time and transcript length polynomial in N on all inputs and executions; overlong or malformed messages are rejected. It has ordinary input access to G,H and no GI oracle. Public coins mean that each verifier challenge consists of newly generated independent uniform bits revealed to the prover; deterministic transcript information is reconstructible from the public input and messages. No verifier randomness is kept hidden. Later random challenges need not be revealed before earlier prover replies. The verifier’s final output is deterministic given the full transcript and all revealed coins. The first message may come from either participant, but the total message count is bounded by a universal constant r, independently of n. There is one prover, no setup, computational soundness assumption or shared secret. P sees the input and messages received so far. A malicious prover may be randomized and use arbitrary computation. On isomorphic pairs, rejection induced by a malicious prover is allowed; producing a different valid isomorphism is still a canonical-soundness error. Thus the guarantee is unconditional probability of output in {s(G,H),⊥}, not a conditional guarantee given that the verifier does not reject.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of a single protocol, canonical selector and P^GI honest prover satisfying all bounds and all three probability requirements, or prove no such protocol exists. An ordinary protocol that verifies an arbitrary isomorphism is insufficient. A public-coin protocol with an unrestricted or stronger honest prover, or a private-coin protocol with a P^GI prover, meets only part of the target. Any fixed canonical selector is allowed; a lower bound just against lexicographic selection would not refute the stated existence question.

context_blocks.title: An isomorphism is easy to check, a canonical one is harder to certify
context_blocks.text: Many permutations can map one graph to another. A pseudodeterministic proof must prevent a malicious prover from choosing which valid answer the verifier produces. The source constructs a protocol that fixes one answer and allows cheating to cause rejection but, with high probability, no alternative answer.

context_blocks.title: Private coins already permit the required prover bound
context_blocks.text: The source’s graph-isomorphism protocol uses a prover that can be implemented in polynomial time with a GI oracle, while the verifier hides randomness. The full version then explicitly asks whether the same prover-complexity bound can be achieved with public coins.

context_blocks.title: Unrestricted public-coin simulation is already known
context_blocks.text: Corollary 7.4 of the full version, corresponding to Corollary 22 in the proceedings, shows that private-coin constant-round pseudodeterministic proofs can be simulated with public coins when the prover has unrestricted power. That equivalence does not preserve the P^GI honest-prover guarantee and therefore does not resolve this card.

context_blocks.title: Later exposition preserves the concrete question
context_blocks.text: Holden’s February 2022 thesis explicitly repeats the public-coin protocol question with a polynomial-time GI-oracle prover after its graph-isomorphism theorem. This pins down the concrete benchmark hidden behind the saved concluding excerpt’s broader question about prover power.

cards.context:
Many permutations can map one graph to another. A pseudodeterministic proof must prevent a malicious prover from choosing which valid answer the verifier produces. The source constructs a protocol that fixes one answer and allows cheating to cause rejection but, with high probability, no alternative answer.

The source’s graph-isomorphism protocol uses a prover that can be implemented in polynomial time with a GI oracle, while the verifier hides randomness. The full version then explicitly asks whether the same prover-complexity bound can be achieved with public coins.

Corollary 7.4 of the full version, corresponding to Corollary 22 in the proceedings, shows that private-coin constant-round pseudodeterministic proofs can be simulated with public coins when the prover has unrestricted power. That equivalence does not preserve the P^GI honest-prover guarantee and therefore does not resolve this card.

Holden’s February 2022 thesis explicitly repeats the public-coin protocol question with a polynomial-time GI-oracle prover after its graph-isomorphism theorem. This pins down the concrete benchmark hidden behind the saved concluding excerpt’s broader question about prover power.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
